name: Battle of Hastings
info: On 14 October 1066 William, Duke of Normandy, defeated the English army of King Harold Godwinson about 7 miles northwest of Hastings; Harold was killed, and William was crowned king on Christmas Day.

facts.date: Saturday 14 October 1066, from about 9 am to dusk
facts.place: About 7 miles (11 km) northwest of Hastings, close to the present-day town of Battle, East Sussex, England; sources differ on the exact site of the English line
facts.sides: A Norman-French army under William, Duke of Normandy, against an English army under King Harold Godwinson; numbers unknown, with modern estimates of 7000 to 8000 for the Normans among several, and most historians arguing for 7000 to 8000 English
facts.outcome: Harold was killed late in the battle, most of his army retreated or was defeated, and William went on to be crowned king of England on 25 December 1066.

t: Edward the Confessor died childless in January 1066, and Harold had to face three rival claimants, Hardrada and Tostig in the north and William in the south, within a few weeks.
The English fought on foot in a shield wall; the Normans used archers, infantry and cavalry, and probably pretended to flee in order to break the English line.
The battle is known from conflicting accounts, so that even Harold's death, by an arrow in the eye in the traditional version, remains uncertain.
dyk: Although later lists of William's companions exist, only about 35 named individuals can reliably be identified as having been with him at Hastings, and only about 20 named Englishmen with Harold.
ev: Edward the Confessor dies on 5 January; Harold Godwinson is elected and crowned king
Harald Hardrada and Tostig defeat an English army at Fulford on 20 September
Harold defeats the Norwegians at Stamford Bridge on 25 September, and Hardrada and Tostig are killed
William lands at Pevensey on 28 September and builds a wooden castle at Hastings
Harold camps at Caldbec Hill on the night of 13 October
On 14 October the battle is fought from about 9 am to dusk, and Harold is killed
William marches on London, receives the English leaders' surrender at Berkhamsted and is crowned on 25 December
William puts down risings in the north and west, culminating in the Harrying of the North into 1070

sections.background:
In 911 the Carolingian ruler Charles the Simple allowed a group of Vikings under Rollo to settle in Normandy, and they adapted quickly to the local culture, took up Christianity and intermarried. In 1002 King Æthelred II of England married Emma, sister of Richard II, Duke of Normandy, and their son Edward the Confessor spent many years in exile there before succeeding in 1042. He drew on Norman courtiers, soldiers and clerics for support, and he may also have encouraged Duke William's ambitions for the English throne. Edward was childless and in conflict with Godwin, Earl of Wessex, and his sons.

His death on 5 January 1066 left no clear heir. Harold Godwinson, Earl of Wessex and the richest and most powerful English aristocrat, was elected king by the Witenagemot and crowned by Ealdred, Archbishop of York, though Norman propaganda said Stigand performed the ceremony. William claimed that Edward had promised him the throne and that Harold had sworn to accept it. Harald Hardrada, King of Norway, claimed it through an agreement between Magnus the Good and Harthacnut. Harold's exiled brother Tostig raided England in early 1066, and in early September Hardrada invaded the north with more than 300 ships carrying perhaps 15,000 men. They defeated Edwin and Morcar at Fulford on 20 September, and Harold beat them at Stamford Bridge on 25 September.
sections.forces:
The numbers at the battle are unknown. Contemporary writers gave William's army as 14,000 to 150,000, which is highly exaggerated, and a contemporary document claiming 776 ships may be inflated. Modern historians offer 7000 to 8000 men including 1000 to 2000 cavalry, 10,000 to 12,000, 10,000 including 3000 cavalry, or 7500. About half were infantry, a quarter cavalry and a quarter archers or crossbowmen, drawn from Normandy and the rest of France, with large contingents from Brittany and Flanders. He spent almost nine months assembling the fleet and landed at Pevensey on 28 September. Only about 35 named individuals can reliably be identified as present with him.

Some Norman sources give Harold's army as 400,000 to 1,200,000, while English sources seem to understate it. Recent historians suggest 5000 to 13,000, and most argue for 7000 to 8000, a mix of the fyrd and housecarls. The fyrd was the local levy, with one man for every five hides, and England as a whole could supply about 14,000 men for it. The housecarls were full-time professionals with better armour, and most fought with the two-handed Danish battleaxe. The English army was entirely infantry and had few archers. Harold had dismissed his militia and fleet on 8 September, marched north and back, and covered about 200 miles (320 km) south to camp at Caldbec Hill. His army was battered after Stamford Bridge.
sections.course:
Harold's forces took a small, dense formation at the top of a steep slope, with a shield wall of locked or overlapping shields. William arranged three groups: Bretons, with men from Anjou, Poitou and Maine on the left under Alan the Red, Normans under William himself in the centre, and French, Picard, Boulogne and Flemish troops on the right under William fitzOsbern and Eustace of Boulogne, with archers in front, spearmen behind and cavalry in reserve. The fighting began about 9 am. The Norman arrows had little effect uphill, and the infantry and then the cavalry could not break the shield wall. A retreat began, blamed on the Bretons, and a rumour that William was dead spread; the English pursued, and William rode through his men showing his face, then led a counter-attack.

A lull probably followed in the early afternoon. William of Poitiers says the Normans twice used feigned flight, which most historians accept, though some argue the story was invented. The feigned flights did not break the line but probably thinned the housecarls, who were replaced by fyrd, and the shield wall held. Harold died late in the battle, but the sources disagree: the traditional arrow in the eye appears first in the 1080s in Amatus of Montecassino, and the Carmen says William killed him. Harold's death left the English leaderless, the soldiers of his household fought round his body to the end, and the rest began to collapse, with a rearguard action at the Malfosse. The battle was over at dusk.
sections.aftermath:
Casualty figures are unknown. Losses among the Englishmen known to have been present imply a fatality rate of about 50 per cent, though this may be too high. One in seven of the named Normans is said to have died, but they were all noblemen. Orderic Vitalis's figures are highly exaggerated, though his ratio of one in four may be accurate, and Peter Marren speculates that perhaps 2,000 Normans and 4,000 Englishmen died. Harold's body was identified the next day by his armour or by marks on it. The Norman dead were buried in a communal grave not yet found, and the English dead, including Harold's brothers Gyrth and Leofwine, were left on the field, some removed later by relatives.

William expected the English leaders to submit, but the Witenagemot instead proclaimed Edgar Ætheling king, with Edwin, Morcar and Archbishops Stigand and Ealdred. William advanced on London round the coast of Kent, defeated an English force at Southwark, and travelled by the Thames valley, where Stigand submitted at Wallingford, and the English leaders surrendered at Berkhamsted. He was crowned by Ealdred at Westminster Abbey on 25 December 1066. Resistance continued for years, with revolts in Exeter in 1067, an invasion by Harold's sons in 1068 and risings in Northumbria; he ruthlessly put them down, culminating in the Harrying of the North in late 1069 and early 1070, which devastated parts of northern England.
sections.sources:
Because many of the primary accounts contradict each other, it is impossible to give an authoritative description of the battle. The only undisputed facts are that fighting began at 9 am on Saturday 14 October and lasted until dusk. The accounts include William of Jumièges, William of Poitiers, the Carmen de Hastingae Proelio, the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, which names the battle as at the hoary apple tree, Orderic Vitalis, Wace and the Chronicle of Battle Abbey, and the Bayeux Tapestry, probably commissioned by Odo of Bayeux soon after. Many are Norman or written after the event, and English sources may understate Harold's army.

Historians dispute much of it: the site of the English line, which some place at the abbey and newer sources at Caldbec Hill; whether the Normans advanced from Hastings, as most believe, or were already on the field, as William of Jumièges has it and M. K. Lawson argues; whether the feigned flights were deliberate; and how Harold died. The Tapestry shows an arrow in an eye beside a figure struck by a sword, with the caption that Harold has been killed, without saying which figure. Ian Walker thinks an arrow in the eye is probable, and Peter Rex concludes that no one can say how he died. The numbers on both sides are unknown. The battlefield has been altered by the abbey's building, and the English slope is now much less steep.
sections.legacy:
Hastings effectively marked the culmination of William's conquest, though resistance went on. Harold's defeat probably had several causes: the need to defend against two near-simultaneous invasions and his dismissal of the militia on 8 September. Most of the blame probably lies in the battle itself: William was the more experienced leader, the English lacked cavalry, and they erred by pursuing the retreating Normans, which exposed their flanks. Harold's death appears to have been decisive. David Nicolle says William's army showed the superiority of Norman-French mixed cavalry and infantry tactics over the Germanic-Scandinavian infantry tradition.

William founded Battle Abbey on the site, with the high altar said to mark the spot where Harold died, though the foundation more likely was imposed by papal legates in 1070. After the Dissolution of the Monasteries the abbey passed to private owners; in 1976 the government bought the estate, with American donors, and English Heritage now administers it. Annual reenactments draw thousands of people. Some English veterans joined the Varangian Guard in Constantinople and fought the Normans again at Dyrrhachium in 1081, where they were defeated in similar circumstances. Legend held that Harold escaped and became a hermit at Chester, and Waltham Abbey claimed his secret burial.

summary: On 14 October 1066 William of Normandy defeated King Harold Godwinson's English army near Hastings. Harold died late in the day and William was crowned king on Christmas Day. The accounts of the battle conflict, so even how Harold died is disputed, and the sizes of both armies are unknown.
notes: The article's numbers for each army: no contemporary figures are reliable, so the facts line gives 7000 to 8000 for the Normans as one of several modern estimates and for the English as what most argue. The article lists four estimates for the Normans without ranking them, so I wrote 'among several'.
Casualties: I gave Marren's speculation, Orderic's ratio and the 50 per cent figure as the article does; all are uncertain.

The forces section says Harold 'marched north and back': the article says he marched north to Stamford Bridge and then about 200 miles south, and I condensed this. The article also says the army took about a week for the march.

Left out: Halley's Comet, the papal banner, William's mounting delays, the Romney landing, the weapons and armour details, Edith the Fair and Gytha stories, the Malfosse detail beyond one line, the lunar and sunset times, the Domesday name of the battle, the Senlac name's origin, the skeleton found at a medieval cemetery, Wace's report of Harold's order.
